The rescue operation fundamentally addresses two distinct classes of mathematical inconsistencies within the software manifold: boundary condition singularities and state-space desynchronization. First, the conformal quantile operator exhibited a breakdown regime when the input rank exceeded the sample size $n$. In continuous mathematics, this might approach an asymptote, but in discrete computational systems, returning $+\infty$ introduces an unbounded scalar that propagates catastrophic errors through downstream Bayesian inference engines. The prescribed fix implements a 'fail-closed' boundary condition, effectively truncating the domain and mapping out-of-bounds inputs to a safe, finite default. This preserves the topological integrity of the probability space.

Second, the red tests in PR #884 revealed a severe base-drift artifact. The test suite contained a stale copy asserting legacy clamping behavior, completely decoupled from the actual source code evolution on the `main` branch. This represents a failure in the synchronization of the system's dual representations: the executable logic and its verification kernel. By identifying that the symbol did not exist on `main` and only resided on the feature branch, we isolated the blast radius. The resolution involved injecting the missing boolean flags into the mock factories, restoring isomorphism between the test environment and the production dependency graph. The empirical verification—transpiling via esbuild and achieving a 36/36 pass rate against hand-computed values—confirms that the corrected operators now reside strictly within their defined validity regimes.
